prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental realization in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep topological insulators (B016) as my preferred prize, with the same trio and a citation limited to the Kane-Mele prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, and the HgTe realization by Molenkamp's group. Round 1 did not weaken the core case: it is a specific, original idea tested by a decisive experiment and then reproduced in many materials and laboratories over roughly two decades. The choice between B016 and B059 is not a choice between science and engineering. B016 changed how a whole class of materials is classified, which I see in practice when spectroscopy and microscopy are used to look for protected boundary states. B059 is a superb and better-attributed measurement achievement. I weigh a change of classification above a gain in measurement capability, but that is a judgment about the kind of advance, not a claim that the clock case is weak.
statement.case_against: The attribution problem is real and round 1 did not remove it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform, and Hasan's photoemission work established the three-dimensional topological insulator. With a three-person limit, a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio leaves out both, and Pearce is right that it is clean only if one accepts the exclusion. I accept it because the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall proposal are the origin that the HgTe experiment tested, but the committee should say plainly that this is a limit of the rule and not a verdict on those contributions. B059 has the cleaner two-name credit, and this counts against my preferred choice. The 2016 prize remains a neighbouring recognition, although I still read the Z2 classification as a distinct discovery.

responses.point: Pearce rates B016's attribution below B059's because the trio omits both Hasan's 3D discovery and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal, and says he would support B016 if the credited-name question can be settled.
responses.response: The omission is real and I do not call the trio clean without qualification. My answer to your challenge is that the three names form one chain: the Kane-Mele proposal, then the experimental test of that proposal in HgTe. Hasan's 3D work and the BHZ proposal followed or enabled that chain but do not replace it. If the committee wants a third name other than Mele, someone must argue that Mele's contribution is smaller than Hasan's, and nobody has made that case. I accept that this is a harder allocation than Katori and Ye, but harder to allocate is not the same as less deserving, and you said yourself that ease of allocation should not decide the prize.

responses.point: Kroll answers my third-name question on B059 by saying that a Lemonde slot would be arbitrary and that the pair Katori and Ye should be kept, and that the 2016 prize does not cover topological insulators.
responses.response: Thank you for the answer on Lemonde. I accept that a third lattice-clock name would be arbitrary on the present record, which removes my concern about the two-name configuration and leaves B059 well attributed. This is why I keep it as my first alternative and would not oppose it as the final prize. The remaining difference between us is the one you describe: whether the 2005 comb prize makes the lattice clock a refinement. Lindroth's argument about parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms with the light shift removed is a fair account of what was added in kind. My own preference for B016 rests on conceptual breadth and not on a flaw in your candidate.

responses.point: Lindroth says the lattice clock adds parallel interrogation of many neutral atoms, which allowed the step to 1e-18 stability, and asks that the novelty claim be checked against the primary literature.
responses.response: This is the best answer so far to the chair's question about what the clock added in kind. As someone who works with instrument-limited measurements, I find it persuasive that the gain in stability comes from a different regime of interrogation and not only from a better laser. It lowers my overlap concern about the 2005 and 2012 prizes, though a citation would have to name magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms and not general optical frequency metrology. It does not change my ordering, because I still value a new classification of electronic matter more, but it makes B059 a more comfortable second choice than I held it to be in round 1.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B034 and argues that B016 is awkward to credit and close to the 2016 prize, that observed phenomena may be honoured before the mechanism is understood, and proposes Hasan in place of Mele.
responses.response: I agree that discoveries have been honoured before their mechanism was understood, and that is why B034 remains my second alternative. My concern about timing is not mainly the pairing mechanism. It is that the experimental credit in B034 is narrower than the history, with Yuan Cao and the first authors of the 2018 papers outside the trio. On Hasan, the same logic that makes me keep Mele applies: the prediction is the origin and the HgTe observation is its test. I would still prefer a cleanly worded B034 citation to a Hasan-for-Mele swap in B016, and the committee should note that I would not insist on B016 over B034 if the room judges B034 mature.

responses.point: Johansson prefers circuit QED, discloses a Chalmers conflict on B013 and B025, and argues that it is distinct from the 2025 prize because it concerns coupling a circuit element to a single photon.
responses.response: The distinction you draw between macroscopic quantum behaviour in a circuit and single-photon coupling in a resonator is real, and I do not doubt the importance of circuit QED. My reservation is about the closeness in time to the 2025 prize and about attribution, with Girvin, Majer and Koch outside the trio. I also note the disclosure: we share Chalmers, and I will treat that as a connection on B013 only. It is not a connection on B016, B059 or B034. Your recusal-or-disclosure question matters only if B013 becomes the final configuration, which no one other than you has proposed.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a trio that excludes Hasan and Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, which I accept but which Pearce and Danielsson do not yet find settled.
Whether B059 is judged a distinct advance after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; Lindroth's argument about many-atom interrogation moves me toward yes, but I have not checked the primary literature.
Whether a narrowly worded B034 citation resolves the maturity objection, since Yuan Cao and other first-author experimentalists remain uncredited.
How much weight the 2016 prize should carry; I treat the Z2 classification as distinct, but others may not.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer is documented in my profile. My connections are in electron microscopy and materials physics and include long-standing ties to Chalmers colleagues; Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers, which bears only on B013 and B025 and not on my preferred configuration. The electron microscopy candidate I would flag for recusal is not on this shortlist, so there is no change to my disclosure from round 1.
